newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Cambodia takes spotlight as Burma, Laos join ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia takes spotlight as Burma, Laos join ASEAN.

text.p: Burma and Laos formally joined the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Wednesday, but the spotlight was on Cambodia as ASEAN foreign ministers debated how to deal with a prospective member they still regard as unstable.
The ministers met for three hours from midday to discuss Cambodia and a bid by Foreign Minister Ung Huot to assuage ASEAN concerns over the turmoil in his country.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told a brief news conference after the meeting that ASEAN reaffirmed its decision to postpone Cambodia's membership in the group, now enlarged to nine with the admission of Burma and Laos.
"We feel there is still instability in Cambodia, and we reaffirmed our decision (of July 10) not to induct Cambodia on the 23rd," he said.
ASEAN, celebrating its 30th year, now comprises Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei, Burma and Laos.

A senior ASEAN source said it was highly unlikely Cambodia would be admitted in the near future. He said it was more likely to happen during an annual ASEAN summit in December if the situation in Cambodia was straightened out, "although in politics anything can happen".
Badawi said the foreign ministers of Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines would meet Ung Huot and then report back to a full ministerial meeting.
An ASEAN source said there was still some question over Ung Huot's status as head of Cambodia's observer delegation at the group's annual two-day foreign ministerial meeting opening on Thursday.
"That is something still to be clarified also," the source said.

Badawi said ASEAN still regarded Prince Norodom Ranariddh as first prime minister despite his ousting on July 5 by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has given ASEAN conflicting signals on Phnom Penh's membership.
Ung Huot has been named to replace Ranariddh, who on Tuesday urged ASEAN not to accept the foreign minister as Cambodia's representative.

The lengthy midday session and Badawi's subsequent news conference delayed the formal induction of Burma and Laos by at least 30 minutes. ASEAN brushed aside Western criticism of Burma's record on human rights and democracy to bring it into the fold.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas discussed Cambodia on Wednesday with U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy, former congressman Stephen Solarz.

"We very much want to work with our friends in ASEAN and other countries in the region," Solarz, who is on an Asian trip to help find a solution to the Cambodian issue, told reporters after the meeting.
Alatas also told reporters he and Solarz had agreed "that we should continue to keep in touch with one another and to cooperate with one another".
Alatas showed a flash of anger when asked why Burma should be allowed to join ASEAN and Cambodia kept out.

"Clearly, objectively, something has happened in Cambodia...has resulted in fighting, in instability, in turmoil in Cambodia, and we in ASEAN asked ourselves whether in that condition Cambodia...could assume its rights and responsibilities as a full-fledged member," he said.
No such conditions prevailed in Burma, he said.
Four demonstrators gathered outside a fast-food shop near the conference hotel on Wednesday to protest on behalf of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma against Rangoon's accession.
Under strict Malaysian laws, five or more people need a permit to demonstrate.
The Network said in a statement Burma's admittance was "a mark of shame to people of the region who value human rights, justice, democracy and peace".
